answers.answer: Caching could reuse the frequently requested, slowly changing guides and avoid their 80 ms database work on hits, at a 2 ms lookup cost. Use station:{stationId}:language:{language}, because languages produce different results. On a hit the API returns the stored guide. On a miss the API reads/builds the guide from the database, writes a copy to the cache, and returns it; the cache does not fetch it itself. A miss still pays the database work plus the cache lookup and fill. Caching also adds storage and operations to expire, remove, or update copies; the database remains authoritative. Acceptable staleness still needs defining.

evidence.quote: The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the result from the database on its own.
Include the inputs that change the answer.
The application finds a usable entry under the requested key and returns the stored result.
No usable entry exists. The application reads the database, stores a copy in the cache and returns the result.
Creating the copy still costs work: fetch or compute the result, then write it to the cache. Storage, lookups and keeping copies current all have costs.

answers.answer: C receives the old hours. B deleted the key before A stored its previously fetched old value, so deletion did not prevent a later stale refill. The team cannot claim every read after B finishes sees the new hours. For this endpoint, bypass the cache and have each request read the authoritative database; under the stated commit prerequisite this avoids serving that stale cached copy. The lesson does not specify a concurrency protocol that fixes this refill race.

evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.
Choose results that are expensive enough to obtain, frequently reused and able to tolerate a defined amount of staleness. Keep freshness-critical decisions tied to authoritative data.

answers.answer: In A, 12:03 can return the original forecast, although the source changed at 12:02. At 12:11 the original entry has expired, so the API must fetch the source and fill again. In B, memory eviction removed the entry at 12:04, so 12:05 must fetch the source even though the original TTL would not end until 12:10. The ten-minute TTL bounds how long that entry may remain usable; it neither refreshes the source automatically nor promises ten minutes of freshness or residence. Eviction frees memory and can happen before expiration.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the data every minute; a later miss must load it again.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.
An entry can be evicted before its TTL ends.
Removes entries to make room. A least-recently-used policy favors removing entries that have not been read recently.

answers.answer: Use one shared cache entry: with no concurrent fills, deleting it removes the copy all four instances use. Today local lookups happen inside each API process, and deleting the writer instance's copy leaves the other three copies intact; requests to those instances can receive old maps. Shared lookups go over the network to a separate service, adding the accepted 2 ms and operational cost. Losing one local cache affects only that instance; the other instances retain their own copies. An unreachable shared cache removes cache access for all four instances. Sharing alone does not keep data current; the writer must still delete the shared entry after the database update.

evidence.quote: Lives inside each API process. Reads avoid a network call, but each process fills and updates its own copy. Their copies can reflect different versions of the same data.
Several API servers use a separate cache service, such as Redis or Memcached. They can reuse entries, but each lookup adds a network call and the service needs operating.
Restarting one API process discards its local cache; other processes keep their copies. If the shared cache is unreachable, every API server using it loses access to those cached entries.
Sharing reduces separate copies. It does not automatically keep the cache current with the database.

answers.answer: Single-key expiration can make concurrent requests repeat the same database lookup, overwhelming the 500 reads/second capacity. Coalesce readers: let one lookup load the schedule while concurrent requests wait for and share its result, then fill the cache, rather than each issuing a database read. During the separate outage, sending all 10,000 requests/second to the database would be 20 times its safe capacity. Limit total fallback reads across instances to at most the safe 500/second and return temporary errors for excess requests; this explicitly bounds database work. If a last-known schedule is independently accessible, requests can reuse it only while it meets the allowed 60-second staleness limit, avoiding database reads; otherwise use the bounded fallback/error path. Permission to serve stale data does not establish that a copy remains accessible when the entire cache is unreachable, and the lesson does not specify where to retain such a copy.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same key together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the application permits stale results.
Falling back to the database is a load decision, not a free recovery path.

answers.answer: Do not add this cache now. Every result is read exactly once, so filling it after that read yields no future hits and avoids no database reads. The 2 ms database read is small relative to the 100 ms budget, and ten reads/second is comfortably within the stated capacity. Cache fills add writes, storage, and management cost; a lookup-before-read design would add misses too. Reconsider if the same results begin receiving frequent repeated reads, especially if retrieval becomes expensive or database load approaches capacity, and define acceptable staleness before adopting it.

evidence.quote: If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.
Choose results that are expensive enough to obtain, frequently reused and able to tolerate a defined amount of staleness. Keep freshness-critical decisions tied to authoritative data.
Creating the copy still costs work: fetch or compute the result, then write it to the cache. Storage, lookups and keeping copies current all have costs.
